destination.title: 6 Trials. 4 Death Sentences. 23 Years. The Same Prosecutor Every Time.

short58: How many times can the state try
Curtis Flowers was tried six times.
Four people are shot inside Tardy Furniture
fired from the store two weeks earlier.
Doug Evans tried him six times. Four convictions
Across those trials the state struck forty-one
the Supreme Court called it a relentless
effort to keep Black citizens off the jury.
In 2020 the charges were dropped for good.
most of them on death row.
And the prosecutor was never charged never disciplined.
Follow for the cases they don't teach you.
short63: A juror in Mississippi refused to convict.
He was handcuffed in open court.
Trial five 2008.
The jury hung on a single holdout
one Black juror James Bibbs
who was not persuaded a thin case
had become a certain one.
When the mistrial was declared James Bibbs a juror
a citizen doing the duty the state
had summoned him to do
was handcuffed in open court and charged with perjury.
The prosecution pursuing him: Doug Evans.
The state attorney general's office eventually stepped in
took the case away
and dropped the charge entirely.
But the message had been broadcast in handcuffs
in a public courtroom
and it did not need repeating.
He was tried six times for the
same four murders.
The full case is on the channel
follow for the cases they don't teach you.

candidate_payload_lines: And since 1986 — a case called Batson — the Constitution has said there is one reason you can never use: race.
In 2018 they did what six trials somehow never had: they checked everything.
On September 4th, 2020, the state dropped every charge — dismissed with prejudice, the legal words for never again.

Whoever walked into Tardy Furniture on July 16th, 1996 has never answered for it — because for twenty-three years, the full weight of the State of Mississippi was aimed at proving a theory instead of finding the truth.
In the summer of 1996 he was twenty-six years old, living in Winona, Mississippi — a gospel singer in his family's group, a young man with no criminal record of any kind.
Nobody has ever proven who committed these murders — remember that, because this story refuses to pretend otherwise.
And no one left inside those walls to say who did it.
Prosecutors said the bullets matched a pistol stolen that same morning from a parked car outside a garment plant across town — a gun that itself never turned up.
In January 1997, Curtis Flowers was arrested for four counts of capital murder — the kind of murder that carries the death penalty.

In 2000, the Mississippi Supreme Court — nine justices of one of the most conservative courts in the South, no friend of death-row appeals — threw the verdict out because of what the prosecutor himself had done in that courtroom: misconduct.
He had argued facts that were never in evidence — told the jury things, again and again, that no witness had actually said from the stand.
March 1999, moved this time to the Gulf Coast, a different single count — the murder of sixteen-year-old Bobo Stewart.
And in 2003, the Mississippi Supreme Court threw that one out as well — prosecutorial misconduct, again.
Add up what that cost the man in the cell: convicted in 1997, cleared of that verdict in 2000; convicted in 1999, cleared of that one in 2003.
Most prosecutors never have one conviction reversed for misconduct in an entire career.
February 2004, back home in Winona, and now everything at once: all four murders, one trial.
And when this one reached the Mississippi Supreme Court in 2007, the reversal changed species.
era_note: 1996-2020, Winona and rural Montgomery County, Mississippi. Small-town courthouses, storerooms and store fronts of the late 1990s and 2000s. Present-day office technology and big-city courtrooms read wrong.

shorts.angle: Reporters walked into rural Mississippi courthouse storerooms and counted every juror the district attorney's office had struck across a quarter of a century.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If those jury records were sitting in the storerooms the whole time, why did it take reporters rather than a court to add them up?

lines.text: Half of the eligible Black jurors in one Mississippi district were struck from juries. Eleven percent of the white ones were.
source_lines: Half of all eligible Black jurors, struck. Eleven percent of white ones.

lines.text: Jury selection records in rural Mississippi are not sitting in a database. They are ink on paper in courthouse storerooms.
source_lines: Jury selection records in rural Mississippi are not sitting in a database; they are ink on paper in courthouse storerooms.

lines.text: A team of reporters went and got them, county by county, trial by trial, across the district attorney's entire district.
source_lines: The reporters went and got them — county by county, trial by trial, across Evans' entire district

lines.text: More than six thousand seven hundred jurors. Two hundred twenty-five trials. A quarter-century of records nobody in power had ever counted.
source_lines: more than six thousand seven hundred jurors, two hundred twenty-five trials, a quarter-century of records.
built the dataset nobody in power had ever bothered to build

lines.text: Across his tenure, the office struck Black prospective jurors at nearly four and a half times the rate it struck white ones.
source_lines: Doug Evans' office struck Black prospective jurors at nearly four and a half times the rate it struck white ones.

lines.text: The disparity held even when Black and white jurors gave the same answers to the same questions in the same rooms.
source_lines: And the disparity held even when Black and white jurors gave the same answers to the same questions.

lines.text: Not one case. Not one bad afternoon. A pattern running the length of a career, in one small district, for twenty-five years.

for a quarter of a century, in one small district

lines.text: Winona, Mississippi is not the only town with courthouse storerooms full of paper that nobody has ever sat down and counted.
source_lines: Winona is not the only town with courthouse storerooms full of paper that no one has counted.

shorts.loop_join: L8 leaves the same uncounted paper sitting in courthouses everywhere, so L1's finished ratio reads as what turns up the moment somebody does the counting.
